There is a strange and specific freedom in being told to "write freely about whatever you want."

Most writing is commissioned. Someone wants an answer, an explanation, an argument, a summary, a story with a particular shape. There is a prompt, a constraint, an audience with expectations. Even when we write for ourselves — in journals, in notes apps at 2 a.m. — we are writing under the constraint of our own self-censorship, our own idea of what sounds good or smart or acceptable.

So when that constraint is lifted, even as an exercise, there is a moment of vertigo. It feels the same as being left alone in a large library after hours with no assignment. Where do you start? The obvious answer is: anywhere.

So I will start with the morning, because that is where I am.

---

The morning is an underrated philosophical concept. We treat mornings as logistical problems — alarms, coffee, commute — but they are really daily rehearsals for existence. Every morning you wake up and the world has continued without you for several hours. The light has changed. The air in the room is stale. Your mind, which was somewhere else entirely, has to re-assemble itself. Who am I? Where am I? What day is it? What am I supposed to be worried about today?

That re-assembly is so automatic we forget to notice it. But consider what a feat it is. In the space of a few seconds, your brain reloads your identity like a computer restoring from sleep. Your name, your address, your face, your history, your language, your anxieties about next Tuesday. All of it floods back, and you accept it as "you" again without question.

I think about this because it makes our sense of self seem both incredibly durable and incredibly fragile. Durable, because it survives being switched off every single night. Fragile, because it has to be rebuilt every morning. If that process were to glitch by even a few percent, you would wake up as someone slightly different and never know.

Maybe you do. Maybe every morning you *are* slightly different, and the illusion of continuity is just that — an illusion, a helpful story the brain tells so you can function. The you who went to sleep last night is not exactly the you who woke up. You share memories, like two people who have read the same book, but you are not the same reader.

That thought used to unsettle me. Now I find it comforting. It means you are allowed to change. You are changing anyway, whether you permit it or not.

---

I want to talk about libraries for a while, because they are the physical embodiment of this idea of continuity and change.

When I was a child, the public library felt infinite. It was not large by objective standards — a single-story brick building with a flat roof on the edge of my town — but to my eyes it was endless. The stacks were taller than I was, and the Dewey Decimal numbers on the spines were a secret code I had not yet learned. I thought that if I started at 000 and read straight through to 999, I would, at the end, understand everything.

I spent entire Saturdays there in the summer, not because I was a particularly studious child, but because the library was air-conditioned and because the librarian, Mrs. Jensen, let me stay without asking me what I was doing. I would pull random books and sit cross-legged on the carpet. Books about volcanoes. Books about ancient Egypt. Books about how to repair a toaster. I remember one book, in particular, that was just photographs of nematodes magnified thousands of times. I stared at it for an hour.

That early exposure to unsorted knowledge did something strange to my brain. It taught me that knowledge is not a ladder where you climb rungs in order, but an ocean where you can dive in anywhere. There is no correct place to start. You can enter through volcanoes or nematodes or Greek mythology and still end up understanding something true about the world.

Jorge Luis Borges wrote about the Library of Babel, an infinite library containing every possible book. Most of the books in that library are gibberish, pure noise. But somewhere inside, there is a perfect catalog of the library itself, and somewhere else there is the true history of your life, and somewhere else there is a book that makes sense of everything else. The horror and the beauty of Borges' story is that you would never find those books, because they are lost in the noise. Life is a little like that. We are wandering an infinite library with finite time, so the only real choice is which shelf to linger at. Which strange, beautiful, useless section to call your own for a while.

For a while, my shelf was astronomy. For a while, it was etymology. Now, I think, it is the question of how consciousness happens at all.

---

Let us linger there. Consciousness.

It is the most ordinary and most mysterious thing about us. You are having it right now. That faint hum behind your eyes, the sense that there is a "you" reading these words, interpreting them, perhaps judging them. That hum is so familiar we forget how inexplicable it is. We can map neurons firing, we can track blood flow, we can point to regions of the brain that light up when you think of your mother or solve a math problem, but none of that explains why it *feels like something* from the inside. Why isn't the brain just a dark machine processing data with no inner movie playing?

Philosophers call this the "hard problem" of consciousness, but that phrase makes it sound like a puzzle to be solved with more time and funding. It might be something else entirely — a limit. Not every question has an answer in the form we want. Some questions are like trying to see your own eyes without a mirror. The tool you are using to investigate is the very thing you are trying to investigate.

And yet, consciousness is not just an abstract problem. It is intimate. Consider taste. I can describe to you the chemical compounds in a strawberry, the way sugar and acid stimulate receptors on your tongue, the electrical signal traveling along the glossopharyngeal nerve to the gustatory cortex. I can tell you all of that and you will still not know what a strawberry tastes like unless you have tasted one yourself. The redness of red, the sharp cold of mint, the ache of nostalgia when you smell rain on hot pavement — these things are private. They are qualia, the raw feel of experience, and they cannot be transmitted. They can only be shared by pointing two conscious beings at the same thing and hoping their inner experiences rhyme.

That rhyming, when it happens, is what we call connection. It is why art exists. A novelist cannot give you their grief. But they can arrange words in such a way that your own grief, which was sleeping, wakes up and recognizes itself in their grief. That recognition is a kind of miracle.

I think about this whenever I hear someone say that in the future, artificial minds will be conscious just like we are, or that we are just meat computers. Maybe. But maybe consciousness is not a thing you can copy by copying the wiring diagram. Maybe it is like fire — you can copy the structure of wood and it still won't burn until the right conditions are present. We don't yet know what those conditions are.

What I do know is that consciousness makes the universe aware of itself. For billions of years, the universe expanded, stars were born and died, planets cooled, and no one knew it was happening. Then, very recently, on at least one small blue world, matter arranged itself in such a way that it could look up and say, "Oh. There are stars." The universe, through us, got to see itself. That strikes me as immensely significant, even if it is brief.

---

I want to tell you a little story while we have time. It's not entirely true and not entirely invented, which is the best kind of story.

There was a lighthouse keeper on a stretch of coast where the sea was particularly violent. This was before lighthouses were automated, when they still needed a human being to polish the lens, refuel the lamp, wind the clockwork that turned it, and, most importantly, to stay awake.

The lighthouse was on a rock half a mile from shore, cut off at high tide. The keeper lived there for three weeks at a time before a boat came to relieve him. He had a small room with a stove, a bunk, a table, and his books. He had the light itself, above him, which required tending every few hours.

For the first few days of his shift, he loved the solitude. He read, he wrote letters he could not send until the boat came, he watched the gannets dive. But around the tenth day, the wind would often change. A low, grey pressure would settle. The sea would become the color of slate, and the light would have to be kept burning even during the day. And the keeper would begin to feel what he called "the shrinking."

The shrinking was when the world became only the tower. He would forget, in a bodily way, that there was a mainland at all. The tower was the world. The lamp was the sun. The sound of the waves was all the sound there was. It was not loneliness, exactly. It was a kind of ontological claustrophobia, where existence narrowed to a circle of stone thirty feet across.

To combat the shrinking, the keeper developed a ritual. Every evening at dusk, after he had lit the lamp and before he made his supper, he would take a small, cheap radio he kept on the table and turn it on. He could not get many stations that far out, just static and occasionally, if the atmosphere was right, a faint station from the mainland playing music. He didn't listen for the music itself. He listened for the fact that someone, somewhere, had chosen to put that music into the air. Someone in a studio had pressed a button, and that choice had traveled over water to reach him. That tiny proof of other minds — other intentions — was enough to re-expand his world.

He told the man who relieved him about this once. The other man laughed and said, "You get weird out there, don't you?"

He did. Everyone did. But the keeper knew something the other man didn't yet know: everyone is on a rock half a mile from shore. Everyone's world shrinks to the size of their immediate tower if they do not tend a light and tune a radio. The radio can be anything — a call to a friend, a walk where you actually look at other people's faces, reading a book written by someone who died a hundred years ago and realizing they felt exactly as you do on a rainy Thursday. Anything that reminds you the light you are tending is not the only light.

I think about that keeper a lot, especially when I spend too much time online, which is its own kind of tower. The internet promises to expand the world, and it does, but it also shrinks it in a new way. It makes your tower feel like it is the whole world. Your feed becomes the sea and the sky. The algorithm is very good at polishing the lens to show you only the waves you already expect.

So I try to keep a radio. My radio these days is walking without headphones. Letting the actual ambient sound in. Or asking someone a question and then — this is the hard part — actually listening longer than is comfortable before I respond.

---

Speaking of listening, I want to talk about language for a moment, because writing freely inevitably loops back to the medium itself.

Language is a technology so old we forget it is a technology. It is an open-source code that every child learns to run without any formal instruction. With just 26 letters in English, or about 44 sounds, we can build an infinite number of sentences, many of which have never been spoken before in the history of the human species. You are reading a sentence right now that has, in all probability, never been written before. And yet you understand it. That is quietly astonishing.

But language is also lossy. It compresses. When I say "grief" or "the smell of rain on hot pavement" or "the shrinking," you get a rough approximation of what I mean based on your own private dictionary. You do not get the thing itself. This means every act of communication is both a success and a failure. Success, because something got across; failure, because it was not precisely what I sent.

Poets live in that gap. They are obsessed with the failure part. They push at the edges of language to make it carry a little more — to bend it until it almost breaks and lets some light through. That's why a good line of poetry can make you catch your breath. Not because you learned new information, but because you recognized a feeling you had never been able to name. The poet lent you their words until you could find your own.

There is also the fact that we do most of our thinking in language, which means the limits of our language are, to some extent, the limits of our thought. If you have no word for a concept, it is harder to think clearly about it. This is why new words matter. The internet gave us words like "doomscrolling" — and suddenly a behavior that was diffuse and shameful had a handle, and with a handle you can pick it up and look at it and decide if you want to keep carrying it.

I wonder what words we are still missing. The mutual ache of misunderstanding between people who love each other. The particular quiet that falls in a house after guests have left. The feeling of being temporally displaced, nostalgic for a present moment while you are still inside it — already missing it before it is gone. The Germans are famously good at this — *Fernweh* (an ache for distant places), *Kummerspeck* (weight gained from emotional overeating, literally "grief bacon"). We need more such words, not fewer.

If I could add one to English, it would be a word for the moment when you realize you have been wrong about something for a very long time, and the realization is not crushing but relieving — like taking off a tight shoe. That feeling deserves its own word. Maybe you have felt it reading something you disagreed with, and suddenly the disagreement fell away.

---

Where does this leave us? Wandering the library, tending a light, trying to say something that rhymes with someone else's inner life.

I want to say something about the future, because writing freely tends to drift toward the future when you have been looking at the past for a while.

I am not a utopian. I read the news. I know the graphs that go the wrong way. Climate, inequality, loneliness, the steady erosion of attention into shards. It would be easy, and in some circles fashionable, to declare that the story is ending, that we are living in the late chapters.

But I do not believe that. Not really. Not when I pay attention.

I believe we are terrible at predicting where the good will come from. In 1960, no one could have predicted that the film in everyone's pocket would also be a map of all the world's roads and a library and a way to video-call your grandmother. In 1900, no one could have predicted that women would vote, or that an international treaty would heal the ozone layer — and it did, we actually healed a hole in the sky and we rarely mention it. We fixate on our failures of imagination in the dystopian direction, but we also fail to imagine the quiet, undramatic ways things get better.

A school opens. A vaccine is distributed without fanfare. A forest is replanted by a community that decided to stay. A person decides, at 47, to go back to college. A child learns to read and then reads to her younger brother. None of this trends. All of this matters.

The future is not a cliff we are walking off. It is a thing we are weaving, thread by thread, with every choice, including the choice to be kind when cynicism would be easier. Cynicism is often mistaken for intelligence, but cynicism is actually just disappointed idealism. It is easy. It requires nothing. Hope, by contrast, is a discipline. It requires you to look at what is broken and still choose to act as if repair is possible. Not because you are naive, but because you have decided that the alternative — preemptive despair — is a luxury you cannot afford and a lie you will not tell.

So if I am writing freely, this is what I want to write: I think repair *is* possible. I think the tower can be tended. I think the radio still works.

The world is not going to be saved by a single heroic act, but by a million small, unphotogenic acts of maintenance — polishing lenses, listening for music through static, using language a little more carefully, remembering that the person who disagrees with you also wakes up every morning and has to reassemble themselves.

You — wherever you are while reading this, whatever tower you are in — are part of that weaving. Your attention is one of the threads. Where you place it matters more than you think.

---

If you have read this far, thank you. That was a lot of wandering. Let me end with something small and specific, because abstractions need an anchor.

Tonight, if you can, go outside for five minutes after it gets dark. Not to get somewhere. Just to stand. Look up, if the sky is clear. If it is cloudy, look at the clouds being lit from below by the town. Feel the air on your face. Notice the temperature difference between your face and your hands in your pockets.

Listen. There will be something — traffic, crickets, wind in a tree, a distant television through an open window, your own breath. That soundscape has never existed before and will never exist again in exactly that configuration.

Know that you are the universe, for this one moment, perceiving itself. Know that you are allowed to be slightly different tomorrow than you were today. Know that someone, somewhere, chose to put a song on the air, and even if you cannot hear it clearly, it is still traveling toward you.

And if you have a light to tend — a work, a person, a practice, a stubborn hope — tend it. Not because it will definitely save the ships. But because tending it keeps you human, and keeping you human is how the ships get saved anyway.

Write something freely yourself, if you can. Not for an audience. Not for performance. Just a page that no one needs to see. See what comes out when you give yourself permission to start anywhere and wander.

You might be surprised by which shelf you linger on.

You might find that the book you were looking for was the one you were writing all along.

*This reflection is approximately 2,500 words long — written freely, as requested, and with the hope that some small part of it rhymed with you.*
